extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of aesthetics; philosophers, artists, architects, sculptors, and painters
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical guidelines for evaluating and producing works in architecture, sculpture, painting, landscape-gardening, and drama, emphasizing how different arts express the Platonic 'Idea' and the objectification of will (beauty, grace, character).

rubrics_metrics.name: Matter cannot itself express an Idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Matter as such cannot be the expression of an Idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matter is merely causality and the substratum of phenomena; perceptible Ideas appear only as qualities of matter. Therefore artists must recognize that matter alone (bare material) does not present an Idea — the Idea is revealed only through qualities and arrangement. Anti-pattern: expecting raw material alone to convey the Idea without form, arrangement, or perceptible qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture should reveal low-grade Ideas (gravity/rigidity)
rubrics_metrics.description: If architecture is regarded as a fine art, its aim is to bring to greater distinctness those Ideas which are the lowest grades of the objectivity of will — such as gravity, cohesion, rigidity, hardness, and light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architecture's æsthetic material is the conflict between gravity and rigidity; the work should prolong and make visible that conflict (e.g., roof presses earth through columns, arches transmit loads via pillars). The beauty of a building lies in the obvious adaptation of every part to the stability of the whole: positions, dimensions, and forms must have necessary relations so that each part bears just as much as it conveniently can. Anti-patterns: gratuitous forms or ornaments that do not follow structural ends; twisted columns (tasteless) that violate simplicity; materials masquerading as other materials (sham building).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form must follow end/function in architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of each part must not be determined arbitrarily, but by its end, and its relation to the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the column is the simplest form of support; frieze, rafter, roof, and dome explain themselves from their immediate end. Decorative capitals belong to sculpture, not architecture. Anti-pattern: decorative forms that obscure or contradict the part's structural purpose (extraneous ornamentation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Material honesty is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure in architecture depends on immediate knowledge through perception of its matter (weight, rigidity, cohesion); discovery that material is different diminishes pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a building appearing to be stone is actually pumice or wood, the relation between rigidity and gravity is altered and the building seems a sham (like a poem in an unknown language). Thus architects should preserve perceptible truthfulness of materials. Anti-pattern: façades or finishes that deceive the beholder about true material and structural behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity and symmetry are subordinate, not primary
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularity of the building and its parts partly aids comprehension and can enhance beauty, but is of subordinate value; symmetry is not invariably demanded (ruins can be beautiful).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design for legibility and revelation of forces rather than rigid adherence to symmetry. Use regular figures to facilitate comprehension but avoid treating symmetry as the chief concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for light and climate in architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Works of architecture have a special relation to light; they gain different beauties in sunshine and moonlight, so special attention is paid to effects of light and to the climate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design should consider how strong light reveals parts and how mass and form unfold the nature of light (interception, reflection, shadow). Choice of forms must suit local climate (e.g., Gothic forms in northern climates constrained by necessity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance æsthetic ends with utility and necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture is often subordinated to useful ends; the architect's merit consists in achieving æsthetic ends despite subordination to foreign utilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select forms of æsthetical beauty compatible with the building's use (temple vs palace vs prison). Where necessity constrains form (harsh climates), compensate by appropriate borrowed ornaments (e.g., sculpture in Gothic). Anti-pattern: forcing a purely aesthetic scheme that ignores functional constraints or producing ornament incompatible with use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Landscape-gardening aims for multiplicity, separation, and fitting connection
rubrics_metrics.description: The landscape beauty of a scene consists in the multiplicity of natural objects, their clear separation, distinct appearance, and fitting connection and alternation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Landscape-gardening assists these conditions but has less mastery than architecture; it's limited in what it can do against unfavourable nature. Anti-pattern: attempting to impose rigid, architectural control over landscape where nature resists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Landscape and still-life painting prioritize subjective contemplation
rubrics_metrics.description: In paintings of still life, mere architecture, ruins, interiors, etc., the subjective side of æsthetic pleasure is predominant — satisfaction lies in pure, will-less knowing rather than direct comprehension of the Idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such works should invite quiet contemplative perception and convey the reflective peace of the observer rather than dramatize high Ideas. Use of painter's eye to reflect serenity is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal painting/sculpture should express species-character (objective side)
rubrics_metrics.description: Animal painting and sculpture give predominance to the objective side of æsthetic pleasure: the characteristics of species (form, action, position, mien) are paramount, not individual character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent animals in forms and actions that reveal their species' character — restlessness, impetuosity, or other strong traits — often with a naivety and openness that arouses interest. Anti-pattern: attributing individual human-like quirks that obscure the species character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical (human) painting/sculpture: express the Idea where will is most objectified
rubrics_metrics.description: The great problem of historical painting and sculpture is to express directly and for perception the Idea in which the will reaches the highest grade of its objectification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These arts should foreground the objective Idea (humanity, moral or historical significance) and subordinate mere subjective contemplation. Aim to make the 'Idea' manifest in action, character, and composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human beauty: anticipate the Ideal (a priori) and combine species with individual
rubrics_metrics.description: Human beauty is the fullest objectification of will at the highest grade knowable; art must anticipate the Ideal a priori and not merely imitate particular beautiful parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The artist must anticipate the Idea (the Ideal) and, using experience as model, realize a whole that surpasses nature (greek canon as example). In portraying humans, separate species-character (beauty) from individual character; represent the individual ideally so that character assists revelation of the Idea. Anti-pattern: piecemeal empiricism (assembling beautiful parts from different people) or failing to anticipate a unifying Ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance species-beauty and individual character (avoid caricature or meaninglessness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character (individual) must be Ideal — significant in relation to humanity's Idea — so beauty is not destroyed by character nor character by beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If individual character annuls the species character → caricature; if species character annuls individual character → absence of meaning. Sculpture should slightly modify the species ideal by individual prominence; painting may emphasize changing emotion and mien. Aim for a definite individual manner that still reveals the Idea of man.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace as adequate temporal expression of will (movement and pose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grace is the adequate representation of will through its temporal manifestation: every movement performed and every position assumed in the easiest, most appropriate and convenient way — the pure, adequate expression of its intention without superfluity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grace presupposes proper proportion and a symmetrical, harmonious figure; it excludes aimless bustle and wooden stiffness. It is essential for brutes and men (not plants), and demanded in acting, sculpture, and painting of motion. Anti-patterns: exaggerated, purposeless movement; stiffness that makes action appear constrained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculpture's principal concern: beauty and grace; avoid phenomena whose essence is non-visual
rubrics_metrics.description: In sculpture, beauty and grace are the principal concern; certain phenomena (e.g., cries/shrieks) lie outside its province because their essence is sound, not mere form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to represent shrieking in marble: the essence of shrieking lies in sound, so portraying the distorted mouth sacrifices other expressive features and produces a ridiculous continuous effort. If expression requires non-visual media (sound, temporality), choose poetic or histrionic arts instead. Example: Laocoon should not be depicted as crying out — sculpture can show the mouth stuck (vox faucibus haesit) but not the sound; depicting futile effort without effect becomes ludicrous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Painting's sphere: countenance, gestures, eyes, and colour for character
rubrics_metrics.description: Painting has the peculiar sphere of the special character of the mind (emotion, passion, alternations of knowing and willing) which must be represented by countenance and gestures; eyes and colour contribute much to beauty and are essential to character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use facial expression, gesture, and colour to convey passing emotion and psychological character. Unlike sculpture (which benefits from multiple viewpoints), the expression/character in painting is often comprehended fully from one vantage point — plan composition accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art requires an a priori anticipation (the Ideal) combined with experience
rubrics_metrics.description: One cannot recognise and imitate the beautiful purely a posteriori from experience; the artist possesses an a priori anticipation (the Ideal) of what is characteristic and beautiful, which experience helps realize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genius involves an anticipation of the Idea and the intelligence to see the Idea in particulars; the artist uses experience as model to call the dim a priori knowledge into clear consciousness. Anti-pattern: relying solely on empirical collection of beautiful parts (Socratic empiricism) to construct beauty.
